individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper introduces BSD, a biologically inspired learning algorithm that jointly trains a feedforward spiking network (stimulus-to-concept) and a backward spiking network (concept-to-stimulus) by aligning basal and apical membrane potentials via a contrastive ReCo loss. It extends prior biological plausibility criteria with spiking neuron communication and unsigned error signals, and evaluates BSD on image classification, character prediction, time-series forecasting, and image generation using MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, and autoencoders, reporting performance often close to backpropagation.
Strengths: The paper proposes a novel bidirectional spiking distillation framework that jointly trains feedforward and backward pathways with a contrastive ReCo loss, introducing two additional biological plausibility criteria (spiking neurons and unsigned signals) beyond prior work.

Extensive experiments across MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, and autoencoders on classification, forecasting, and generation tasks show BSD can often approach BP performance while being more biologically grounded than several prior algorithms.
Ablation studies (ReCo vs MSE vs InfoNCE, frequency decomposition, threshold/lambda sensitivity) provide useful insights into the design choices.
The appendix provides detailed implementation and gradient derivations, aiding reproducibility.
Weaknesses: Biological plausibility is overstated: training uses non-biological components such as AdamW with global statistics, batch normalization, gradient clipping, cosine schedules, RandAugment, and surrogate gradients; the 'local' learning is still implemented via autodiff and detach, and no neuromorphic or local-plasticity implementation is demonstrated.

The C5 'unsigned error signaling' criterion is not convincingly satisfied: the ReCo loss is computed on continuous voltages and its gradients are signed; the analogy to unsigned reward prediction errors in the brain is not supported by any neural evidence or spiking error encoding.

The claimed 'comparable to backpropagation' is not supported across all tasks: text-character accuracy is ~10 points lower, FID scores are substantially worse (e.g., FashionMNIST 112.97 vs 29.07), and MLP accuracy on MNIST/CIFAR-10 is more than 3-9 points lower; the only clear wins are on some forecasting MSE/MAE metrics.

The comparison setup is potentially unfair/misaligned: BSD uses a dual-pathway architecture with additional parameters, a different output decoding (cosine similarity to target spike trains), and task-specific tricks (FFT frequency decomposition, separate lambda weights), so 'identical architectures' is not convincingly established.

The 'non-two-stage' criterion is not properly validated; PyTorch training still requires a forward and backward pass, and the algorithm uses detach to truncate graphs rather than demonstrating a true online/simultaneous learning mechanism.
The paper lacks theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees, and no evaluation of the memory-recall capability of the backward pathway, despite this being a core motivation.
Notation and equations contain inconsistencies (e.g., Eq. 4's v_i = \hat{v}_i' assignment, confusing primes for Type 1/Type 2 neurons), making the method hard to parse.
Questions: How is C5 satisfied when ReCo loss is computed on real-valued membrane potentials and its gradient is a signed continuous signal rather than an unsigned spike-based error?
Can BSD be trained without autodiff/surrogate gradients and global optimizers such as AdamW? If not, how does this not violate C2 and the biological plausibility claims?
What is the role of the backward network at inference time, and how is memory recall evaluated? If the backward path is discarded, why is bidirectional training necessary?
How are the parameter counts and computational costs of BSD compared fairly with BP baselines, given the extra backward path and different decoding scheme?
Why does BSD-MSE fail to converge on classification but converge on sequential tasks, and does this reveal an issue with the ReCo loss masking optimization instability?
Are the improvements on time-series datasets statistically significant given the reported standard deviations?
Limitations: Reliance on surrogate gradients, global optimizers, and batch normalization undermines the claimed biological plausibility.
The backward pathway's memory-recall ability is not directly measured; the paper only evaluates classification/regression/generation performance.
Scalability to modern architectures (transformers, residual networks, large-scale datasets) remains untested.
The method incurs additional computational and parameter cost due to the dual-pathway architecture; no efficiency comparison is provided.
Performance is still substantially below BP on text prediction and image generation, limiting practical utility.
No theoretical justification for why ReCo loss leads to effective credit assignment or convergence.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper proposes Bidirectional Spike-based Distillation (BSD), a biologically plausible learning algorithm that jointly trains a feedforward spiking network (stimulus-to-concept) and a backward spiking network (concept-to-stimulus) by aligning local basal and apical voltages with a contrastive loss. The authors introduce two additional biological plausibility criteria beyond prior work: spiking neuron models (C4) and unsigned error signals (C5). They evaluate BSD on image classification (MLPs/CNNs), sequential regression (RNNs), and image generation (autoencoders), reporting performance close to backpropagation in some settings and ablating loss functions, thresholds, and weight asymmetry.
Strengths: The idea of jointly training feedforward and backward spiking pathways via local voltage alignment is novel and combines ideas from predictive coding, target propagation, and contrastive learning into a single spiking framework.
The paper formalizes two new biological plausibility criteria (C4 and C5) and explicitly states that BSD satisfies all five, which helps structure the discussion of biological fidelity.
The method is evaluated across diverse architectures and tasks, including MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, and autoencoders, and the authors provide detailed appendices with architectures and hyperparameters.
The ablation studies (ReCo vs InfoNCE vs MSE, penalty weight lambda, firing threshold, weight alignment dynamics) provide useful insights into why ReCo loss works and how the two pathways interact.
Weaknesses: The central claim that BSD achieves performance 'comparable to backpropagation' is not consistently supported: in Table 1, backpropagation-trained SNNs outperform BSD on most CNN benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10 87.02% vs 84.13%, CIFAR-100 57.21% vs 53.48%), and in image generation, BSD's FID is substantially worse than ANN-BP (e.g., FashionMNIST 112.97 vs 29.07).

The local-error criterion (C2) is undermined by the batch-level ReCo loss, which requires computing cosine similarity across all samples in a batch. This is not a biologically local synaptic plasticity rule and requires global access to other samples' activations.

Biological plausibility is overstated: training uses continuous surrogate gradients, AdamW, batch normalization, cosine annealing, and autodetach operations, while only inference uses spikes. The paper does not explain how these floating-point optimization components are biologically justified.

The 'unsigned error signal' criterion (C5) is weakly justified: ReCo loss is nonnegative, but the resulting gradients and weight updates are signed. Moreover, the backward pathway receives one-hot target vectors as supervised labels, which is a global teaching signal.
The notation is confusing and sometimes inconsistent (e.g., v vs \hat v, Type 1/Type 2, top-layer CE loss), making the exact architecture and loss computation hard to follow and reproduce.

The paper does not compare against strong recently proposed biologically plausible SNN training methods (e.g., spike-based target propagation, surrogate-gradient local learning), and it lacks code release despite a reproducibility statement.
Questions: How does the batch-level ReCo loss satisfy the claim of local synaptic plasticity if each neuron's alignment requires cosine similarities against all other samples in the batch?
Does the use of surrogate gradients, batch normalization, and AdamW during training violate the proposed C4 criterion? If so, why is C4 considered satisfied?
What exactly is \hat v_L in the top-layer cross-entropy loss, and how is the one-hot label temporally encoded as spikes?
On which benchmarks is the difference between BSD and backpropagation-trained SNNs statistically significant? The tables show overlapping standard deviations in several cases.
Why is R-STDP marked as satisfying all five criteria in Table 1? Does R-STDP use unsigned error signals and local errors in the same way as BSD?
Could the performance gap to BP-trained SNNs be reduced with more hyperparameter tuning or longer training, especially on CIFAR-10/100 and FID benchmarks?
Does feeding the one-hot target into the backward pathway during training conflict with the goal of avoiding global error signals?
Limitations: Batch-level contrastive loss is not biologically local and requires global batch statistics.
The training algorithm relies on non-biological components such as surrogate gradients, batch normalization, AdamW, and cosine annealing, so only inference is truly spike-driven.
Performance on generative tasks is notably worse than backpropagation-trained ANNs, with FID gaps of 40-80 points on MNIST and FashionMNIST.
The method has not been validated on modern large-scale architectures (residual networks, transformers) or large-scale datasets.
The biological plausibility of providing one-hot class labels as spike trains to the backward pathway is not discussed in depth.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes Bidirectional Spike-based Distillation (BSD), a biologically plausible learning algorithm that jointly trains feedforward and backward spiking networks. Learning is framed as a transformation between stimulus encoding and concept encoding, with feedforward and backward pathways mutually distilling spiking feature representations. The method introduces two additional biological plausibility criteria (spiking neurons and unsigned error signals) and claims to satisfy all five criteria. Experiments cover image classification, text character prediction, time-series forecasting, and image generation, showing performance that is sometimes comparable to backpropagation.
Strengths: The bidirectional spiking framework inspired by perception-recall is a novel conceptual contribution, and using asymmetric weights avoids the weight transport problem.
The paper evaluates BSD across diverse architectures (MLP, CNN, RNN, autoencoder) and tasks, which is a broad empirical scope.
Ablation studies analyze the choice of loss function and frequency decomposition, showing the benefit of the ReCo loss and adaptive penalties.

On some CNN classification benchmarks, BSD is within a few points of backpropagation (e.g., CIFAR-10 84.13% vs. 87.12%), indicating that biologically constrained learning can be competitive in certain settings.
Weaknesses: Biological plausibility claims are overstated: the ReCo loss uses batch-level negative pairs, which requires access to all samples in a batch, and the training procedure relies on surrogate gradients and autodiff, both of which are not biologically local or neuronally plausible. Thus, satisfying criteria C2 (local error) and C5 (unsigned error signaling) is questionable.

Performance is not consistently comparable to backpropagation. MLP results are substantially worse (e.g., CIFAR-10 48.90% vs. 57.65%, CIFAR-100 22.10% vs. 27.92%). Image generation FID on FashionMNIST is 112.97 vs. 29.07 for BP, which is far worse, contradicting the claim of comparable performance.

Table 2 contains mis-bolded entries: BSD is bolded even when it is not the best (e.g., Electricity MSE 0.165 vs. Predictive Coding's 0.162, and Pems-bay MSE 0.174 vs. BP-ANN's 0.164). This misreporting undermines the reliability of the experimental claims.

The inference rule for classification is not biologically motivated: it uses cosine similarity between output spikes and one-hot label spike trains, which is a template-matching scheme rather than a learned decision layer, and it may not scale to more complex or open-set tasks.

The paper has clarity issues: notation is inconsistent and confusing (e.g., v_i, v_i', \hat{v}_i, \hat{v}_i'), layer indices for local losses are inconsistent, and the main algorithm is only in the appendix. Reproducibility is hindered by missing code and incomplete implementation details.

Novelty over existing biologically plausible methods (e.g., CCL, DLL, target propagation) is incremental; the core idea of using contrastive alignment between two pathways is a straightforward combination of known components.
Questions: How can a biological neuron access the full batch of samples to compute the ReCo loss, which includes negative pairs across the batch? What is the neural mechanism for suppressing spurious correlations across samples?

Since the spike function is non-differentiable and BSD uses surrogate gradients, how is this biologically plausible? Does the algorithm require a separate forward and backward pass for gradient computation, which would violate the non-dual-phase criterion (C3)?

Table 2 shows several bold entries where BSD is not the best performer (e.g., Electricity MSE). Please clarify the bold formatting rule and explain how these results support the claim of comparable performance.

For generation tasks, the top-layer Type 2 neurons receive the input image as the target. How does this correspond to the memory recall or concept-to-stimuli reconstruction narrative? Is this simply an autoencoder rather than bidirectional learning?
How were hyperparameters (threshold, lambda, learning rate) selected for each dataset? Was there a separate validation split, or were they tuned on test performance?

The inference procedure uses cosine similarity to one-hot label spike trains. Does this require knowing all class labels in advance, and how does this relate to standard classification? Is this scheme biologically plausible?
Limitations: The method is only tested on small/medium-scale datasets (MNIST, CIFAR, etc.) and shallow architectures; scalability to deeper networks, residual connections, or attention mechanisms is not demonstrated.
No theoretical guarantees are provided for convergence, representational capacity, or why the ReCo loss should lead to effective credit assignment.
The paper does not provide code, making it difficult to reproduce the experiments or verify the exact training and inference procedures.
The inference rule based on label templates may not generalize to tasks without fixed classes, limiting the practical applicability of the approach.
The biological plausibility claims are not carefully hedged; the use of batch statistics, surrogate gradients, and autodiff are not discussed as limitations.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces Bidirectional Spike-based Distillation (BSD), a biologically plausible learning algorithm that jointly trains feedforward and backward spiking networks by mutually distilling spiking feature representations. The method frames learning as a transformation between stimulus encoding and concept encoding, inspired by the brain's perception-recall architecture. The authors propose two additional biological plausibility criteria (spiking neuron model and unsigned error signals) beyond three existing criteria, and claim BSD satisfies all five. They evaluate BSD on image classification, sequential regression, and image generation tasks, reporting performance comparable to backpropagation in some cases while maintaining biological fidelity.
Strengths: The bidirectional architecture inspired by perception-recall is an interesting conceptual contribution that differs from standard unidirectional learning paradigms.

The introduction of two additional biological plausibility criteria (C4: spiking neuron model, C5: unsigned error signaling) extends the criteria framework proposed by Lv et al. (2025) and provides a more complete checklist for evaluating biologically plausible algorithms.

The paper provides extensive experiments across diverse tasks (classification, time-series, text prediction, generation) and architectures (MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, autoencoders), including ablation studies of the loss function and visualizations of learned representations.
Weaknesses: The biological plausibility claim is significantly undermined by the use of non-biological components: training relies on AdamW, surrogate gradients for the spike function, batch normalization, and autodiff-based gradient computation. These are not biologically grounded, so the criteria C2 (local error) and C3 (non-two-stage) are only superficially satisfied; weight updates still use global optimization.

Criterion C5 (unsigned error signals) is not convincingly satisfied: the top-layer loss is cross-entropy (a signed error), and the gradients from the ReCo loss and AdamW produce signed updates. The paper does not explain how unsigned signaling is implemented in the actual learning mechanism.

Performance is not truly comparable to backpropagation: on image generation, BSD underperforms BP by large margins (e.g., FID 72.39 vs 49.56 on MNIST, 112.97 vs 29.07 on FashionMNIST), and on CIFAR-100 MLP classification BSD achieves 22.10% vs 27.92% for BP. These gaps undermine the abstract's claim of 'comparable performance.'

The technical presentation is unclear in key places: notation in Equations (4)-(5) is confusing (e.g., v_i and v'_i are defined in overlapping ways), making it hard to follow the exact flow of feedforward and backward signals. The main text defers critical algorithmic details to appendices without sufficient explanation in the body.

The comparison to FSVAE in image generation is not apples-to-apples, as BSD uses a deterministic autoencoder rather than a variational autoencoder, and the FID differences are substantial, weakening the significance of the generative results.
Questions: Given the reliance on AdamW, surrogate gradients, and batch normalization, which components of this implementation are intended to correspond to biological mechanisms? How can the algorithm be considered biologically plausible when these standard deep learning tools are used without a biological counterpart?

The top-layer loss is cross-entropy, which is a signed error measure. How does BSD satisfy criterion C5 (unsigned error signals) for this loss? Could the authors clarify what exactly is meant by 'unsigned' in the context of the actual gradient updates?

In Figure 7, the feedforward and backward weights are nearly orthogonal except in the final layer. Does this mean the backward pathway does not actually reconstruct intermediate representations? How does the method still achieve classification accuracy without weight alignment in hidden layers?

The performance gaps on CIFAR-100 and image generation are notable. Are these due to the spiking neuron discretization, the local loss objective, or the architecture? Are there plans to scale BSD to larger or deeper architectures (e.g., ResNets, Transformers) to see if the gap persists?

The target is provided as a one-hot spike train to the top-layer Type 2 neurons. How is this biologically plausible? In the brain, top-down signals are not one-hot category labels; what alternative target encodings were considered?
Limitations: The method depends on non-biological components (AdamW, surrogate gradients, batch normalization), which weakens the biological plausibility claim.
The experiments are limited to relatively small-scale datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, etc.) and simple architectures; scalability to deeper and more complex models is not demonstrated.
Image generation quality is clearly inferior to backpropagation, indicating a trade-off between biological fidelity and generative performance that is not fully explored.
The biological inspiration is high-level and not validated by neural data; the mapping from apical-basal alignment to cortical learning remains speculative.

review.Summary: The paper introduces Bidirectional Spike-based Distillation (BSD), a biologically plausible learning algorithm that jointly trains a feedforward and a backward spiking network. Learning is framed as a transformation between two spiking representations (stimulus and concept encodings), using local Relaxed Contrastive (ReCo) losses to align membrane potentials of paired pyramidal-neuron compartments. The authors propose two additional biological plausibility criteria (spiking neuron models and unsigned error signaling) and claim BSD satisfies all five criteria. Experiments cover image classification (MLPs/CNNs), sequential regression (RNNs), and image generation (autoencoders), showing performance often close to backpropagation and competitive with other biologically plausible baselines.
Strengths: The idea of joint feedforward/backward distillation with spiking neurons is novel and clearly inspired by cortical perception-recall loops.
Extensive empirical evaluation across diverse tasks and architectures, including ablations on loss functions and frequency decomposition.
The algorithm is shown to achieve competitive performance on several benchmarks, including superior MSE on some time-series datasets compared to backpropagation.
Detailed appendices provide gradient derivations, hyperparameters, and additional experiments, supporting reproducibility.
Weaknesses: The biological plausibility claims are overstated: BSD still relies on surrogate gradients, automatic differentiation, batch normalization, and likely backpropagation-through-time for RNNs, which lack clear biological analogs.

Criterion C5 (unsigned error signaling) is weakly justified; the ReCo loss is a continuous scalar, and weight updates use signed gradients, while the top-layer cross-entropy loss is a supervised signed error.
The 'spike-based' distillation is performed on continuous membrane voltages rather than spike trains, undermining the claim of spike-based communication for learning.
Performance is not consistently comparable to backpropagation; there are notable gaps on SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, and especially image generation (e.g., FashionMNIST FID 112.97 vs 29.07 for BP).

The comparison is unfair in terms of model capacity: BSD uses two parallel pathways (Type 1 and Type 2) and thus more parameters than standard networks, but baselines are not given a similar capacity increase.

Table 1 shows R-STDP already satisfies C1–C5, contradicting the claim that BSD uniquely satisfies all criteria; the contribution appears incremental relative to existing biologically plausible methods.
The notation is inconsistent (e.g., v'_i is used for both Type 2 basal and Type 1 apical potentials), and the RNN formulation is unclear, hindering reproducibility.

The method does not include comparisons with several recent biologically plausible algorithms (e.g., Forward-Forward, target propagation variants) or standard SNN surrogate-gradient training methods beyond BP-on-SNN.
Questions: How is criterion C5 (unsigned error signaling) exactly satisfied when the ReCo loss is continuous and the top-layer uses cross-entropy, and weight updates are computed via signed gradients (including surrogate gradients)? Does any signed error value ever propagate between neurons?

Are RNNs trained with backpropagation-through-time? If so, how does this satisfy C3 (non-two-stage training)? Are batch normalization and surrogate gradients considered biologically plausible components?

For classification, the inference rule uses cosine similarity between output spikes and label spike trains. How are these computed for multi-timestep spike trains? What is the effect of using a standard readout layer instead?
Do the baselines in Tables 1 and 2 have the same number of trainable parameters as BSD? If not, how do you ensure a fair comparison given BSD's additional backward pathway?
Since R-STDP also satisfies C1–C5 according to Table 1, what is the specific novelty of BSD's biological plausibility beyond improving performance?

The image generation FID for BSD is significantly worse than BP (e.g., FashionMNIST 112.97 vs 29.07). Do you consider this 'comparable'? What architectural or algorithmic changes could close this gap?
In Eq. (4) and (5), the notation for v' and vhat is ambiguous. Could the authors clarify the exact compartments for Type 1 and Type 2 neurons and how the two pathways share information?
Limitations: The algorithm is not fully biologically plausible because it relies on surrogate gradients, autodiff, batch normalization, and possibly BPTT.
The 'spike-based' nature is weakened by aligning continuous membrane voltages rather than actual spike trains.
The additional backward pathway roughly doubles parameters and computational cost, which is not accounted for in comparisons.
Performance gaps are non-trivial on complex datasets and generative tasks; current experiments are limited to shallow networks and do not test scalability to deep/residual/attention architectures.
No theoretical analysis of convergence, stability, or representational capacity is provided.
The unsigned error criterion is based on a single neurophysiological study and interpreted loosely.

review.Summary: The paper proposes Bidirectional Spike-based Distillation (BSD), a biologically plausible learning algorithm that jointly trains feedforward and backward spiking networks by aligning basal and apical membrane potentials through a contrastive ReCo loss. It introduces two additional biological plausibility criteria (spiking neurons and unsigned error signals) and evaluates BSD on image classification, text prediction, time-series forecasting, and image generation using MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, and autoencoders, reporting performance that is sometimes close to backpropagation.
Strengths: The bidirectional spiking framework inspired by perception-recall is a novel conceptual contribution that differs from standard unidirectional learning paradigms.
The paper formalizes two new biological plausibility criteria (C4 and C5), extending the criteria framework proposed by prior work and structuring the discussion of biological fidelity.
Extensive experimental evaluation across diverse architectures (MLP, CNN, RNN, autoencoder) and tasks, with detailed ablation studies on the loss function, thresholds, and weight alignment dynamics.
Detailed appendices provide gradient derivations, hyperparameters, and additional experiments, supporting reproducibility to some extent.
Weaknesses: Biological plausibility is significantly overstated: training relies on non-biological components such as surrogate gradients, AdamW, batch normalization, gradient clipping, and autodiff, while only inference uses spikes.
The batch-level ReCo loss requires computing cosine similarity across all samples in a batch, which is not biologically local and contradicts the claimed local-error criterion (C2).

Criterion C5 (unsigned error signaling) is not convincingly satisfied: the ReCo loss is a continuous nonnegative value, but the resulting gradients and weight updates are signed, and the top-layer loss is cross-entropy, a signed supervised error.

Performance is not consistently comparable to backpropagation: there are notable gaps on MNIST/CIFAR MLP and CNN benchmarks, and image generation FID is substantially worse (e.g., FashionMNIST 112.97 vs 29.07 for BP).

The comparison setup is potentially unfair because BSD uses an extra backward pathway (more parameters) and a different output decoding scheme (cosine similarity to label spike trains) than the baselines.

The notation is inconsistent and confusing (e.g., v and \hat v, Type 1/Type 2 compartments), and critical algorithmic details are deferred to appendices, hindering reproducibility; no code is released.
The paper lacks theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees, and the memory-recall ability of the backward pathway is not evaluated despite being a core motivation.
Questions: How does the batch-level ReCo loss satisfy the claim of local synaptic plasticity if each neuron's alignment requires cosine similarities against all other samples in the batch?
How is criterion C5 satisfied when the top-layer uses cross-entropy and weight updates are computed via signed surrogate gradients? Does any unsigned error signal actually propagate between neurons?
Given the reliance on AdamW, surrogate gradients, batch normalization, and automatic differentiation, which components are biologically plausible and how is C2/C3 satisfied?
What is the exact role of the backward pathway at inference time? Is it used for memory recall, and if not, why is bidirectional training necessary?
Are the improvements on time-series datasets statistically significant given the reported standard deviations and multiple hallucinated bold entries in Table 2?
How are parameter counts and computational costs of BSD compared fairly with BP baselines given the additional backward pathway?
Why does BSD-MSE fail on classification but work on sequential tasks, and does this indicate an optimization instability masked by the ReCo loss?
Limitations: The method is not fully biologically plausible because it uses surrogate gradients, batch normalization, AdamW, and autodiff for training.
The ReCo loss is batch-level and not biologically local, requiring global access to other samples' activations.
The backward pathway's memory-recall ability is not directly measured; the paper only evaluates task performance.
Scalability to modern architectures (residual networks, transformers) and large-scale datasets is untested.
Performance on generative tasks is notably worse than backpropagation-trained ANNs, with FID gaps of 40-80 points.
The dual-pathway architecture increases parameter count and computational cost, but no efficiency comparison is provided.
No theoretical analysis of convergence or representational capacity is provided.
